items.title: The Mint's Doubt
items.question: A mint suspects one of 9 fresh coins is heavier than the rest. What is the fewest balance-scale weighings that guarantee finding it?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — weigh 3 against 3, then weigh the heavy trio one against one.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. First weighing: 3 coins against 3 — the heavy side (or the leftover trio if balanced) holds the culprit. Second weighing: 1 against 1 from that trio. Two weighings always suffice for nine.
items.lessonContent:
Split into thirds: a balance scale tests three groups at once, not two.
Each weighing has three outcomes — left heavy, right heavy, balanced — tripling your resolving power.
Nine suspects collapse to three, then to one, in exactly two rounds.
Powers of three govern every such puzzle.
Share this: grab nine identical coins, mark one secretly, and let a friend find it in two tries.

items.title: Pearls of Weight
items.question: Eight pearls look identical, but one weighs more. How many weighings on a balance scale pin it down for certain?
items.correctExplanation: Right — two weighings resolve up to nine suspects, and eight fits inside that budget.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. Weigh 3 against 3: if one side dips, the heavy pearl is among those three; if balanced, it hides among the leftover two. One more weighing finishes either case. Eight suspects fit comfortably inside the nine that two rounds can resolve.
items.lessonContent:
Capacity thinking beats casework: two weighings resolve any batch up to nine.
Eight pearls fit inside that budget with room to spare.
The first weighing always splits into thirds — 3, 3, and the rest.
Leftovers are free information: balance means the odd one sat out.
Share this: test the 3-3-rest split on any small batch tonight.

items.title: The Unknown Deviation
items.question: Twelve marbles hide one that is either heavier or lighter — you don't know which. How many weighings identify it and tell which way it differs?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — three weighings: the classic twelve-ball puzzle, the hardest fair version of the genre.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. The first weighing (4 vs 4) both locates the odd marble among at most four suspects and encodes its possible direction. Two further weighings disentangle which marble and whether heavy or light. No two-weighing scheme can cover twelve suspects times two directions.
items.lessonContent:
Unknown deviation doubles the mystery: each suspect is really two suspects — heavy-X or light-X.
Twelve balls mean 24 possibilities, and three weighings yield 27 outcomes — just enough room.
The first weighing must also encode direction, usually 4 against 4.
This is information theory wearing a puzzle costume.
Share this: explain tonight why twelve is the magic maximum for three rounds.

items.title: Bars of Doubt
items.question: Twenty-seven gold bars look identical, but one is heavier. Fewest balance weighings to find it?
items.correctExplanation: Right — 9 against 9, then 3 against 3, then 1 against 1: three rounds, each dividing by three.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. Split into three piles of nine: one weighing isolates the heavy pile. Repeat 3-vs-3, then 1-vs-1. Twenty-seven is three cubed, so three rounds resolve it with zero waste.
items.lessonContent:
Powers of three are the natural batch sizes: 3, 9, 27, 81 — each adds exactly one round.
Twenty-seven is the textbook case: three piles of nine, then three of three, then one pair.
Any smaller batch rides free inside the next power's budget.
Recognizing 27 as 3³ is the whole insight.
Share this: stack 27 coins in three piles and run the classic solution by hand.

items.title: Boxes in a Row
items.question: Four identical boxes hide one heavier box. What is the minimum number of balance weighings?
items.correctExplanation: Right — two weighings: the first narrows four suspects to at most two, and the second settles it.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. Weigh 1 against 1: a dip names the heavy box immediately, while balance leaves two suspects for the second round. Four exceeds what one round can cover, so two is both necessary and sufficient.
items.lessonContent:
Four suspects overflow one round's three outcomes, forcing a second weighing.
The leftover strategy shines: sidelined items stay suspects at zero cost.
Necessity and sufficiency are separate claims — prove both.
Counting outcomes before weighing is the professional habit.
Share this: argue tonight why four items need a second round but three do not.

items.title: The Counterfeit Batch
items.question: Ten coins include one counterfeit that is lighter. Fewest weighings to find it?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — two weighings cover only nine; the tenth coin forces a third round.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. Nine suspects fit in two rounds, but the tenth overflows the budget — 3² = 9 < 10. The third weighing handles the spillover. Knowing the counterfeit is lighter doesn't help, because volume, not direction, is the constraint.
items.lessonContent:
Capacity is everything: n weighings resolve at most 3ⁿ suspects when the deviation is known.
Ten exceeds nine, so a third round is forced by arithmetic alone.
The classic trap is assuming 'just one more coin' costs nothing.
Thresholds matter more than totals — 9 versus 10 is the whole story.
Share this: ask someone why ten coins need three rounds but nine need two.

items.title: Eleven Steel Spheres
items.question: Eleven steel balls conceal one heavier ball. How many weighings guarantee finding it?
items.correctExplanation: Right — two rounds cover nine, so eleven needs a third.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. Two weighings resolve at most nine suspects, and eleven overflows that budget. The third round absorbs the extra two with room to spare — capacity jumps to twenty-seven.
items.lessonContent:
Just over a power of three is the most expensive place to sit — eleven costs what twenty-seven costs.
Budget boundaries (3, 9, 27, 81) decide everything before a single weighing.
Smart puzzlers round the batch size up to the next power first.
The gap between 9 and 11 is two balls and one whole extra round.
Share this: price batches of 9, 10 and 11 tonight and feel the threshold bite.

items.title: Thirteen Unknowns
items.question: Thirteen coins hide one that is heavier or lighter — unknown which. Minimum weighings to identify it and its nature?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — three rounds cover only twelve unknowns, so the thirteenth forces a fourth.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. Three weighings yield 27 outcomes, but the unknown-direction cases consume two outcomes each — room for just twelve coins. The thirteenth coin breaks the budget, and a fourth round opens twenty-seven fresh outcomes.
items.lessonContent:
Unknown deviation doubles each suspect: twelve coins mean 24 cases, not 12.
Three rounds give 27 outcomes — enough for twelve unknowns, never thirteen.
The formula (3ⁿ−3)/2 sets every unknown-deviation limit.
Knowing the direction in advance roughly doubles your resolving power.
Share this: explain tonight why the thirteenth coin costs a whole extra round.

items.title: Ingots in Bulk
items.question: Twenty-six ingots include one heavier ingot. Fewest weighings to find it?
items.correctExplanation: Right — twenty-six fits inside twenty-seven, so three rounds suffice with one slot to spare.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. Three weighings resolve up to 27 suspects, and 26 slides under that ceiling. Split 9-9-8: the scale's verdict always leaves at most nine suspects, then three, then one.
items.lessonContent:
Round up to the next power of three first — 26 becomes 27 in your head.
Uneven piles are legal: 9-9-8 still narrows to nine either way.
The ceiling, not the exact count, sets the price.
Most real batches sit awkwardly between powers; the method absorbs it.
Share this: price 26 versus 28 tonight and feel the power-of-three cliff.

items.title: A Dozen Suspects
items.question: Twelve coins hide one counterfeit of unknown deviation. How many weighings resolve it fully?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — the famous twelve-coin puzzle: three weighings, starting 4 against 4.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. Twelve unknowns mean 24 cases, fitting inside 27 outcomes with room for three balanced verdicts. The opening 4-vs-4 split both locates the coin and encodes its possible direction — the puzzle's celebrated crux.
items.lessonContent:
Twelve is the largest unknown-deviation batch three rounds can resolve: 24 cases in 27 slots.
The opening 4-vs-4 does double duty — locating and orienting at once.
Later rounds spend the encoded direction like currency.
This puzzle humbled generations of mathematicians before its solution spread.
Share this: attempt the first weighing's logic tonight before reading any solution.

items.title: One Over Budget
items.question: Twenty-eight identical tokens hide one heavier token. Minimum weighings?
items.correctExplanation: Right — twenty-eight overflows the 27 that three rounds cover, forcing a fourth.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. Three weighings resolve at most 27 suspects, and 28 exceeds it by exactly one token. That single overflow buys a whole extra round — capacity jumps to 81. Thresholds punish stragglers.
items.lessonContent:
One token over a power of three costs an entire extra round.
Twenty-eight needs what eighty-one needs — the cliff edge is brutal.
Always compare batch size against 3, 9, 27, 81 before weighing anything.
Real quality control sizes batches to sit just under powers.
Share this: ask why 27 tokens cost three rounds but 28 cost four.

items.title: Crates in the Warehouse
items.question: Forty crates include one heavier crate. Fewest balance weighings to find it?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — forty sits between 27 and 81, so four rounds are necessary and sufficient.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. Three rounds cover only 27, so forty demands a fourth — which then covers up to 81 with room to spare. Split 13-13-14 to open; every verdict leaves a solvable remainder.
items.lessonContent:
Between powers, always round up: 40 lives in 81's territory, priced at four.
Opening splits need not be equal — 13-13-14 narrows correctly.
The method degrades gracefully for any awkward batch size.
Warehouse-scale puzzles are just the mint puzzle with bigger numbers.
Share this: price any batch tonight by rounding up to the next power of three.

items.title: A Full House
items.question: Eighty weights hide one heavier weight. Fewest balance uses to find it?
items.correctExplanation: Right — eighty slides under eighty-one, so four rounds suffice with one slot spare.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. Four weighings resolve up to 81 suspects, and 80 fits with a single slot to spare. Open 27-27-26 and let the thirds do the work. Sitting one under a power is the cheapest seat in the house.
items.lessonContent:
One under a power of three is the cheapest seat: 80 costs what 81 costs, no more.
Opening 27-27-26 keeps every branch inside budget.
The last slot's emptiness never matters — ceilings cover ranges, not exact counts.
Sitting just under thresholds is a design skill in sampling plans.
Share this: price 80 versus 82 and feel which side of the cliff each sits on.

items.title: Eighty-One Marbles
items.question: Eighty-one marbles hide one heavier marble. Minimum weighings?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — 81 is 3⁴, so four rounds resolve it with zero waste.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. Eighty-one equals three to the fourth, so four rounds of perfect thirds — 27s, then 9s, then 3s, then singles — resolve it exactly. Powers of three are the only batch sizes with zero slack.
items.lessonContent:
Exact powers of three — 3, 9, 27, 81 — resolve with zero waste and zero thought.
Each round divides by exactly three: the platonic ideal of the method.
Every other batch size is priced by rounding up to these landmarks.
Memorize the powers and every weighing puzzle prices itself.
Share this: recite 3, 9, 27, 81 tonight as the four prices of certainty.

items.title: Two-Round Capacity
items.question: With two weighings and a known-heavier oddity, what is the largest batch you can resolve?
items.correctExplanation: Right — two rounds yield 3² = 9 distinguishable outcomes, so nine suspects is the ceiling.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 9. Each weighing triples your resolving power: 3 outcomes, then 3 × 3 = 9 distinct verdict paths. Ten suspects would need a tenth path that does not exist — capacity is exact, not approximate.
items.lessonContent:
Capacity grows as powers of three: n rounds resolve at most 3ⁿ suspects.
Nine is the two-round ceiling — the tenth suspect has nowhere to hide its verdict.
Information theory counts outcomes, not effort.
Design any testing scheme by its outcome budget first.
Share this: explain tonight why ten coins need three rounds but nine need two.

items.title: Three-Round Capacity
items.question: A jeweller receives a shipment where one gem in the lot is heavier. Her contract allows three balance checks. What is the largest lot she can accept?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — three rounds give 3³ = 27 distinct verdict paths, each naming one suspect.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 27. Three rounds of ternary outcomes produce 27 distinct verdict sequences — one per suspect, with none to spare. The twenty-eighth suspect would need a twenty-eighth path that three rounds cannot supply.
items.lessonContent:
Three rounds, twenty-seven paths: 3³ is the ceiling for known-deviation batches.
Each suspect needs its own unique verdict sequence.
Twenty-eight breaks the budget by exactly one — the cliff from the other side.
Outcome budgets decide puzzles before a single weighing happens.
Share this: list what three weighings can and cannot cover, then test a friend.

items.title: Unknown Pair Budget
items.question: Two weighings, unknown heavier-or-lighter: largest batch fully resolvable?
items.correctExplanation: Right — three coins mean six cases, fitting inside nine outcomes with room for balance verdicts.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. Unknown deviation doubles each suspect into heavy-or-light cases: three coins make six cases, fitting inside nine outcomes. Four coins would need eight cases plus balance room — over budget. Small numbers, strict arithmetic.
items.lessonContent:
Unknown deviation doubles every suspect, so budgets shrink fast at small sizes.
Three coins, six cases, nine outcomes — the tightest fair fight in the genre.
The general formula (3ⁿ−3)/2 starts exactly here, at n = 2.
Direction-unknown puzzles punish every wasted outcome.
Share this: try to fit four unknowns into two rounds tonight and watch it fail.

items.title: Unknown Trio Budget
items.question: A customs lab can run only three balance tests per suspect shipment of unknown-deviation coins. What is the biggest shipment it can fully clear?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — twelve unknowns make 24 cases, fitting inside 27 outcomes: the famous ceiling.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 12. Twelve coins of unknown deviation make 24 heavy-or-light cases, and 27 outcomes leave room for the three all-balanced verdicts. Thirteen unknowns would need 26 cases plus balance room — over budget by the symmetry the formula demands.
items.lessonContent:
Twelve is the largest unknown-deviation batch three rounds can resolve — 24 cases in 27 slots.
The formula (3ⁿ−3)/2 governs every unknown-direction limit.
Thirteen breaks it by the symmetry the outcomes require.
This ceiling is why the classic puzzle uses twelve, never thirteen.
Share this: ask why the famous puzzle stops at twelve coins, never thirteen.

items.title: Five Dice
items.question: Five identical dice hide one heavier die. Minimum weighings?
items.correctExplanation: Right — five fits inside nine, so two rounds: 2-vs-2 first, then finish the survivors.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. One round covers only three, so five needs a second — weigh two against two, then resolve whichever pair or leftover the scale points at. Five sits awkwardly between powers but rides free at two.
items.lessonContent:
Awkward batch sizes ride free inside the next power's budget: five costs what nine costs.
Two-vs-two openings leave manageable remainders either way.
Never price by exact count — price by ceiling.
The 4-to-9 band is the cheapest crowded neighborhood in the genre.
Share this: price batches of 4, 5 and 9 tonight and notice the flat rate.

items.title: Sealed Envelopes
items.question: Six sealed envelopes hide one with a heavier coin inside. Fewest weighings?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — six fits inside nine: 2-vs-2 first, then finish among at most three.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. Weigh two envelopes against two: a dip isolates the heavy pair, balance isolates the leftover pair — and any pair resolves in one more weighing. Six rides free inside nine's budget.
items.lessonContent:
Pairs are the natural opening below nine: 2-vs-2 leaves no remainder larger than two.
Every branch of the first weighing must land inside the next round's budget.
Checking all three branches before weighing is professional discipline.
The method works for any container — envelopes, dice, crates.
Share this: run the 2-vs-2 opening on any six objects tonight.

items.title: Spare Batteries
items.question: Seven identical batteries hide one heavier battery. Minimum weighings?
items.correctExplanation: Right — seven fits inside nine: open 2-vs-2 or 3-vs-3, then finish the survivors.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 2. Open 3-vs-3: a dip leaves three suspects, balance leaves one — either finishes in round two. Seven sits two under the ceiling, so every branch stays comfortable.
items.lessonContent:
Near-ceiling batches still cost ceiling price: seven needs two rounds like nine does.
Openings can be 2-vs-2 or 3-vs-3 — both keep every branch solvable.
Flexibility in the first split is a feature, not sloppiness.
The only unforgivable sin is a branch exceeding the next round's budget.

items.title: Sacks of Grain
items.question: Twenty-five sacks of grain hide one heavier sack. Fewest weighings?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — twenty-five slides under twenty-seven, so three rounds suffice.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 3. Three rounds cover up to 27, and 25 fits with two slots spare. Open 8-8-9 and every branch lands inside nine. Near misses of powers still pay full power price — and no more.
items.lessonContent:
Near misses of powers pay full power price — 25 costs what 27 costs, no discount.
Openings like 8-8-9 keep every branch at nine or under.
The two spare slots never matter; ceilings cover ranges.
Real warehouses live in these near-miss bands constantly.
Share this: price 25, 26 and 27 tonight and feel the flat rate.

items.title: A Single Pair
items.question: Two coins hide one heavier coin. How many weighings?
items.correctExplanation: Right — one coin per pan; the heavy side answers immediately.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 1. A single weighing of one against one settles two suspects with no remainder. It is the genre in miniature: every grand solution is this round, repeated.
items.lessonContent:
Two suspects, one weighing: the smallest fair puzzle in the genre.
Every grand solution is this atomic round, repeated and nested.
Starting tiny builds the instinct that scales to eighty-one.
Masters of the twelve-coin classic began exactly here.
Share this: solve the two-coin case aloud before attempting anything bigger.

items.title: Mid-Range Crates
items.question: Forty crates include one heavier crate. Minimum weighings?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — forty sits between 27 and 81, so four rounds are necessary and sufficient.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 4. Three rounds cover only 27, so forty demands a fourth — which then covers up to 81 with room to spare. Split 13-13-14 to open; every verdict leaves a solvable remainder.
items.lessonContent:
Between powers, always round up: 40 lives in 81's territory, priced at four.
Opening splits need not be equal — 13-13-14 narrows correctly.
The method degrades gracefully for any awkward batch size.
Warehouse-scale puzzles are just the mint puzzle with bigger numbers.
Share this: price any batch tonight by rounding up to the next power of three.

items.title: Four-Round Unknowns
items.question: A factory's QC protocol allows four balance checks on parts whose defect could run either direction. What is the maximum lot size it can certify?
items.correctExplanation: Right — (81−3)/2 = 39: four rounds yield 81 outcomes, minus balance room, halved for two directions.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is 39. Four weighings give 81 verdict paths; reserving the all-balanced outcomes leaves 78, and each unknown coin consumes two — one heavy-case, one light-case. Thirty-nine is the exact ceiling, forty breaks it.
items.lessonContent:
The general formula (3ⁿ−3)/2 governs every unknown-direction limit.
Four rounds: 81 outcomes, minus balance room, halved — 39 coins exactly.
Each unknown coin spends two outcome paths, heavy-case and light-case.
This single formula prices the entire genre's hard mode.
